paper_title: From Large Language Models to Efficient System One Models via Adaptive Computation

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Transferring LLMs into System One decision models typically replaces the language modeling head with a decision head while retaining the full backbone, making every decision pay for all layers. Yet it remains unclear how much depth such decisions require. We find that decision information is concentrated in intermediate layers, with early layers building essential features and the final six layers removable without loss, while independently trained smaller models largely mimic the full model rather than developing specialized decision capabilities. These findings suggest that efficiency requires not simply smaller backbones, but shared computation across different depths. Building on this, we propose \method{}, which jointly trains a full model with prefix sub-models that share its final layers and decision head through self-distillation. A lightweight gate reads the hidden state at each exit to determine whether additional computation is needed, allowing one model to operate at multiple layers. Across seven decision benchmarks, our approach matches or outperforms independently trained models at every depth, while achieving better accuracy-efficiency trade-offs through adaptive computation.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Dual-process theories distinguish fast, intuitive System One thinking from slow, deliberate System Two thinking (Kahneman, 2011). LLM-based agents increasingly require both. Alongside long chain-ofthought reasoning, they make frequent, lightweight decisions, such as routing requests, selecting tools, flagging unsafe prompts, and recognizing intents, often under tight latency constraints (TypeSafe AI, 2026). System One decision models address this need by fine-tuning an LLM to predict distribution over candidate options at single position, Preprint. Work in progress. Figure 1: Left: Accuracy versus computation depth for independently trained models, and NESTONE w/o the stop gate. Right: Average depth of the gate versus the share of easy decisions; on the four largest benchmarks, accuracy stays within 0.1 points of the fixed 24-layer exit. All models use Qwen3.5-4B and the same training data; models are averaged over 3 seeds. without generating tokens (InternLM Team, 2026; Li and Wang, 2026). For example, Intern-Decision4B, built on Qwen3.5-4B (Qwen Team, 2026), achieves 90.0% macro accuracy across seven decision benchmarks. However, replacing the language modeling head with decision head leaves the full backbone intact: every decision still traverses all 32 layers, incurring latency of approximately 1.45 ms per layer at batch size one in our setting. This raises fundamental question: how much computational depth does System One decision actually require? Fine-tuning is necessary to equip an LLM with decision capabilities that its base model lacks (Section 3), but whether all inherited layers are necessary remains unclear. natural way to reduce inference cost is to truncate the backbone, trading computational depth for potentially lower accuracy. As shown in the left panel of Figure 1, this trade-off is highly non-uniform: reducing the model from 32 to 24 layers largely preserves performance, whereas further truncation causes substantial degradation, with accuracy dropping from 84.3% to 72.8% and 61.5% at 16 and 12 layers, respectively. This highlights the limitation of fixed-depth inference, which imposes the same computational budget on all inputs. Yet, not every decision requires the same amount of computation. This motivates adaptive depth allocation (Figure 1, right), which allows computation to stop once sufficient depth is reached, reducing inference cost while preserving accuracy. We find that decision computation is concentrated in intermediate layers, while independently trained smaller models largely replicate the full model rather than develop specialized decision capabilities (Section 3). First, decisions emerge within narrow band of middle layers: integratedgradient attribution places 50% of the decision by layer 20 and 80% by layer 23. Consistently, ablating layers 2429 leaves accuracy unchanged, while ablating layers 1523 eliminates the decision margin (Section 3.1). Second, independently trained smaller models behave more like truncated full models than independent specialists: 8992% of their correct decisions are already made by the full model, and their distinct wins exceed full-model seed disagreement by only 23 points, mostly on low-confidence decisions (Section 3.2). These findings show that training smaller models or truncating the backbone alone is insufficient. Instead, decision models should learn to make reliable decisions at multiple depths, adapting computation to input difficulty. Based on these findings, we propose NESTONE, framework that transforms an LLM into multidepth System One decision model. NESTONE jointly trains the full model and nested prefix sub-models with shared final layers and decision head, combining decision supervision and selfdistillation from the full model. This enables single training run to produce multiple exits within one checkpoint. At each exit, lightweight gate reads the hidden state to determine whether further computation is needed before producing the decision. Our contributions are threefold: (i) We show that decision information is concentrated in intermediate layers and that independently trained smaller models largely reproduce, rather than specialize in, the full models decisions; (ii) We propose NESTONE, nested multi-depth training framework that combines decision supervision, self-distillation, and hidden-state stopping gate for transfering from LLMs to System One Models efficiency; (iii) We demonstrate that NESTONE matches or outperforms independently trained models at every depth while reducing inference cost through adaptive early exiting, using single training run to obtain multiple models.

sections.title: 2 Background and Related Work
sections.content: System One Decision Models. System One models take state, typed question, and set of options, and return distribution over the options in single forward pass without generating text (TypeSafe AI, 2026). Following Jev, growing number of such models are built by adapting pretrained LLM. Open recipes read the option-symbol logits of an instruction-tuned LLM at the last position, with no training, or add LoRA adapters and decision head initialized from the language-model head (Geuter et al., 2026). Intern-Decision (InternLM Team, 2026) fully fine-tunes Qwen3.5 (Qwen Team, 2026) at 0.8B, 2B, and 4B parameters, Microsoft-Decision1 is post-trained from Qwen3.5-9B (Microsoft, 2026), CLM trains decision model contrastively from Qwen3-8B (Kwok et al., 2026), and CS1 trains 4B model on 12 million clinical decisions (Zhang et al., 2026). Other work changes how options are read out. Jeva encodes the request and each option separately so that the decision is permutation-equivariant, can abstain, and can reuse option states across requests (Li and Wang, 2026); Prism-1 scores each option in its own attention block so that neither option order nor added rivals change the result (Teng et al., 2026); and Considerthen-Choose removes order dependence at inference without training (Huang et al., 2026). Evaluating System One Models. second line of work asks where System One models can replace LLMs. System1-Arena compares ten System One models with open and closed LLMs through shared decision interface and finds that the fast models suffice for many single-step decisions but fall behind on long-horizon tasks (Chen et al., 2026). Other studies evaluate System One models as decision points in agent harnesses (Li, 2026), and test their transfer to low-resource languages (Fadli et al., 2026). These studies treat each model as black box and measure what it outputs. Layer Pruning. The deeper layers of LLMs are known to be partly redundant. Removing block of late layers costs little on question answering (Gromov et al., 2024; Men et al., 2024), and merging or pruning layers followed by distillation recovers most of the original accuracy at smaller size (Yang et al., 2024; Muralidharan et al., 2024; Xia et al., 2024). These methods produce one smaller model with one fixed depth, and they select layers by similarity or importance scores computed for generation rather than by where decision is computed. Existing work on System One models focuses on how to train an LLM into decision model, whether through readout design, training data, or architecture, and on how the resulting models behave. Each of these models keeps the full depth of its backbone, and cost is reduced only by choosing smaller backbone. To our knowledge, no prior work asks where inside the LLM the decision is computed, or what smaller decision model learns relative to the full one. We address both questions first (Section 3). The answers then guide an efficient way to turn one LLM into System One model with several depths: nested prefix training with self-distillation, and gate that reads the hidden state before the readout is computed (Section 4).

sections.title: Models
sections.content: We investigate what enables an LLM to become System One decision model by comparing the model before and after decision fine-tuning, along with smaller variants obtained by progressively removing layers from the fine-tuned model. Specifically, we ask two questions: (i) Where in the network are decisions computed (Section 3.1)? (ii) What do smaller models learn compared to the full model (Section 3.2)? Setting. We study Qwen3.5-4B (Qwen Team, 2026), whose 32 layers we index 031, and InternDecision-4B (InternLM Team, 2026), released decision model built on the same backbone. To establish controlled reference, we re-train Qwen3.5-4B using the same training recipe as Intern-Decision4B. We refer to this re-trained model as full32, which serves as the starting point and reference for all our models. Specifically, full32 is fully finetuned with cross-entropy on the option symbols (AdamW, learning rate 2 106 with cosine decay, 2 epochs, about 131K tokens per step) on 44,941 decisions drawn from public training splits (Zhang et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2024; Lin et al., 2023; Ji et al., 2023; Casanueva et al., 2020; FitzGerald et al., 2023; Clark et al., 2019) and deduplicated against all test states. It reaches 84.3 0.2% over three seeds, compared with 90.0% for InternDecision-4B, whose larger training set covers the J-Hard and Typed benchmarks better. We consider two layer-cutting strategies: middle cut, Mk, which retains layers 0, . . . , k3 and the final two layers (3031), and tail cut, Tk, which retains only the first layers (0, . . . , k1).

sections.title: 3.1 The Decision Is Written at Mid Depth
sections.content: When Does the Decision Become Readable? We examine when the decision-related information emerges among layers and when it becomes accessible to the models own readout. At each layer, we extract the residual state at the readout position and evaluate it using two complementary methods. The logit lens (Nostalgebraist, 2020) applies the models final normalization and output head to the intermediate state, measuring whether the model can already produce the correct answer at that depth. In contrast, linear probe (Alain and Bengio, 2016), trained to predict the gold option from the same state, measures how much decisionrelevant information is linearly recoverable, regardless of whether the models own readout can access it. Thus, the gap between the probe and logit-lens accuracies indicates information that has been encoded in the residual stream but is not yet usable by the models output head. Figure 2(a,b) shows consistent pattern across the base model and Intern-Decision-4B. At layer 15, the probe substantially outperforms the logit lens (76.1% vs. 26.2% for the base model; 77.9% vs. 38.3% for Intern-Decision-4B), indicating that decision information is already encoded but not yet accessible to the models readout. This gap closes over layers 1923: for Intern-Decision-4B, the probe reaches 90.1% at layer 20, matching its final accuracy (90.0%), while the logit lens rises from 64.4% at layer 19 to 89.4% at layer 23. The two readouts then differ by only 0.1 points (vs. 2.8 points for the base model). Neither improves beyond layer 23, suggesting that layers 2431 add no linearly recoverable decision information. Finetuning raises the probe plateau by about seven points (89.5% vs. 83.2% at layer 23) without shifting the depth at which decisions become readable. Which Layers Shape the Decision? Consequently, layers 2429 contribute only 5% net, primarily rescaling the margin without changing the preferred option. Overall, the middle layers play the dominant role in shaping the final decision distribution of fine-tuned System One model. Which Layers Can Be Removed? Table 1 evaluates layer importance through two complementary interventions. First, we remove layers without retraining (Table 1a), using middle cut Mk or tail cut Tk. Second, we perform joint mean ablation (Table 1b): for each layer ℓ, we estimate its mean contribution ℓ across token positions and approximately 1,700 decisions (up to 400 per benchmark), then replace each layers contribution with this mean at every position. This preserves the residual streams typical scale while removing decisionspecific information. Joint ablation measures the groups collective contribution to decision-making, accounting for interactions among its layers while preventing them from compensating for one another. We report the resulting change in mean margin and accuracy over 348 decisions. The two interventions reveal distinct layer roles. In Intern-Decision-4B, removing layers 2429 without retraining leaves accuracy unchanged, while removing layers 2431 costs only 0.6 points. Similarly, full32 retains 84.4% accuracy under T24, compared with 84.2% uncut; cutting into the middle band is substantially more damaging, with T22 losing 11.6 points. Mean ablation confirms this pattern: jointly ablating layers 2429 slightly improves margin and accuracy, whereas ablating layers 1523 eliminates the entire margin and reduces accuracy by 57.8 points. Early layers, however, remain essential despite their small direct margin contributions: ablating layer 0 costs 46.6 points and layer 6 costs 7.8, reflecting their role in constructing features used by later layers. Consistent with this, 16-layer model trained only on layers 821 and 3031, the layers most affected by finetuning, achieves just 35.7%, compared with 73.8% for the M16 prefix model. Takeaway. decision-tuned LLM writes its decision in band of middle layers (1523) on top of feature-building early layers, and its last body layers carry no decision.

sections.title: 3.2 Diagnosing Decision Behavior
sections.content: We next examine what independently trained smaller models learn relative to full32. We finetune M24, M16, and M12 using the same data and recipe as full32, obtaining 83.5%, 73.8%, and 62.9% accuracy, respectively. We compare their predictions with full32 decision by decision, categorizing each as both correct, only full32 correct, only the smaller model correct, or both incorrect. To establish noise floor, we also compare full32 against two independently trained seeds (43 and 44), which uniquely solve 1.42.0% of decisions missed by the reference seed (Table 2, top). Moreover, they lose substantially more decisions than they uniquely solve, by roughly factor of three to four (1,012 vs. 352 for M16; 1,513 vs. 425 for M12). Unique Correct Predictions Are Rare and Uncertain. M16 and M12 uniquely solve only 3.8 4.3% of decisions, just 23 points above the noise floor. These wins are low-confidence (median confidence 0.590.61; full32 gold probability 0.23 0.33) and concentrated in Typed and AGNews (78%), with none in J-Easy or J-Orig. Noise-floor disagreements show the same pattern: median confidence of 0.520.55, with 7173% from Typed and AGNews. Smaller Models Also Lose Reliable Decisions. When full32 assigns the gold option probability 0.8, M24, M16, and M12 achieve 99.7%, 84.1%, and 70.4% accuracy, respectively, while other full32 seeds reach 100%. When full32 is confidently wrong (p < 0.2), smaller models recover only 1720% of these decisions, compared with 0.70.9% for other seeds. Their apparent gains therefore reflect greater disagreement with full32, rather than systematic correction of its errors. Overall, smaller models reproduce many of full32s correct decisions but lose substantial reliable capability without consistently correcting its mistakes. Figure 3: Overview of NESTONE. (a) Nested training with self-distillation. Prefix exits share the full models weights and final block. The full model learns from the gold option y, while each sub-model learns from both and the full models distribution. (b) Adaptive inference with stop gates. The model runs layer by layer, with lightweight gate evaluating the hidden state at each intermediate exit. If ge τ , it runs the final block and returns decision; otherwise, it continues from the saved states without recomputation. Takeaway. Smaller decision models trained on their own do not learn different solution; they learn degraded version of the full models. This suggests training them as parts of the full model, sharing its weights and using its own output distribution as target, so that each smaller model inherits as much of the full models skill as its depth allows.

sections.title: 4 Methodology
sections.content: Section 3 shows that intermediate layers already encode sufficient information to identify the correct option, while smaller decision models are best viewed as prefixes of the full model that should learn to imitate it. Building on these findings, NESTONE trains nested prefix sub-models within the full model using self-distillation to facilitate information sharing across depths (Sections 4.1 and 4.2). lightweight gate then selects the exit depth for each decision based on question difficulty (Section 4.3). with the decision head the coda = head f31 f30. An exit after layer reads out the decision distribution pe( x) = softmax(cid:0)C(h(e))O/Te (cid:1), where is the set of option symbols and Te is temperature fitted per exit. The sub-model Sk with layers uses the exit after layer ek = k3, eg. S12, S16, and S24 exit after layers 9, 13, and 21, and S32 is the full model. This design follows Section 3.1. Prefixes keep the early feature-building layers that no smaller model can do without, and S24 reaches into the decision band while dropping the late layers that carry no decision. The coda is shared so that every exit reads out through the same final layers and head. Because each sub-model is prefix of the next, the states computed for shallow exit are reused when decision continues to deeper exit, so stopping early never requires recomputation.

sections.title: 4.3 Choosing Depth per Decision
sections.content: A single checkpoint now offers exits at intermediate depths, as well as the full model. To choose an exit for each decision, we attach lightweight gate to each intermediate exit. The gate reads the hidden state ze at the readout position immediately after the corresponding middle layer: ge(x) = σ(cid:0)w ze + be (cid:1), where σ is the sigmoid function. Each gate is logistic regression model trained to predict whether its corresponding exit answers correctly, using labels ce = 1[arg max pe = y] and class-balanced weights. At inference, the model runs layer by layer. At each intermediate exit, it stops if ge(x) τ , runs the coda, and returns arg max pe; otherwise, it continues from the saved states. The final exit always answers. Answering at exit costs + 3 layers: the prefix plus the coda. Because the gate reads the hidden state before the coda, evaluating it requires only dot product and sigmoid operation. single threshold τ is shared across exits and selected on held-out data as the most aggressive value for which macro accuracy remains within δ points of always exiting at the final intermediate depth.

sections.title: 5.1 One Checkpoint versus Separate Models
sections.content: One Checkpoint Matches or Outperforms Separate Models at Every Depth. Table 3 compares the four exits of NESTONE with independently trained models at matching depths. No exit performs significantly worse, while the shallower exits achieve higher accuracy. The largest gain occurs at 12 layers (64.4% vs. 61.5%, +2.9 points), with confidence interval excluding zero even when resampling seeds. At 16 layers, the gain is 1.8 points but does not reach significance. The 24-layer exit achieves 83.7%, comparable to M24 (+0.2 points) and full32 (0.6 points), while using 25% fewer layers and reducing latency from 46.5 to 34.7 ms. At 32 layers, accuracy is only 0.3 points below full32, indicating that joint training imposes little cost on the full model. Thus, single 80-minute training run replaces four separate runs while yielding the best accuracy at 12, 16, and 24 layers. sections.title: 5.2 Choosing Depth per Decision
sections.content: The Hidden State Predicts Whether an Exit Is Correct. We first measure how well each signal separates correct from wrong answers at an exit, using AUROC on the test halves. The state gate reaches 0.86, 0.89, and 0.88 at exits 9, 13, and 21, against 0.85, 0.86, and 0.84 for the calibrated top probability, and 0.86, 0.86, and 0.84 for the confidence gate that combines top probability, margin, and entropy. The hidden state thus carries more information about correctness than the exits own confidence, especially at exit 13 and 21, and it is available before the coda is computed. Stopping Rules. We compare the state gate with three rules based on the exit distribution pe: Maxprob, which uses the calibrated top probability; confidence gate, logistic regression on the top probability, top-two margin, and entropy; and State + confidence, which combines these features with the hidden state ze. All rules use the same training labels, class-balanced weights, and fitting data. They evaluate exits 9, 13, and 21 in order, stopping at the first score above τ or answering at exit 21 otherwise; τ is selected as in Section 4.3. The key difference is inference cost: distribution-based rules must run the coda to obtain pe, adding two layers at each checked exit, whereas the state gate reads ze before the coda and runs it only once, at the selected exit. Fixed exits 13 and 21 serve as references. The State Gate Gives the Best Trade-off. Table 4 compares the gating rules at two accuracy thresholds. The state gate achieves the lowest average depth at both δ = 0.25 and δ = 2, using 21.6 and 20.2 layers, respectively, compared with 24 layers for the fixed exit. On hard benchmarks, it uses 23.924.0 layers, whereas confidence-based rules incur two additional layers per readout, resulting in an average depth of 26.627.9 layers. On the four largest benchmarks, which account for 96% of decisions, the state gate preserves the fixed-exit accuracy, with changes of only +0.08 and +0.03 points at the two thresholds. The other rules also remain within 0.13 points of the fixed exit, but achieve savings differently: confidence-based rules save computation on easy decisions while spending more on hard ones, whereas the state gate reduces depth on easy decisions (to 20.2 and 17.5 layers) without incurring additional computation on hard decisions. Randomly mixing exits 13 and 21 to match the same average depth instead reduces accuracy by 3.0 and 4.7 points. The Accuracy Drop Is Concentrated on Small Benchmarks. The state gates macro-accuracy drop (1.56 and 1.68 points) comes almost entirely from the three smallest benchmarks, which contain only 430 of 12,351 decisions but account for three of seven macro-averaged benchmarks. At δ = 0.25, it misses seven additional decisions on these benchmarks but loses none on larger ones. Compute savings depend on traffic mix: average depth ranges from 24 layers on hard-only traffic to 20.2 on easy-only traffic (22.1 for an even mix), and to 17.5 layers at δ = 2 (20.7 for an even mix; Figure 1, right). Since the selected threshold varies across training splits (0.80 vs. 0.92), it should be calibrated on held-out deployment-like traffic. Adding the full model as final exit further improves the trade-off: at δ = 2, the gate matches its accuracy on the four largest benchmarks (0.01 points) while using 23.9 layers on average, 19.8 on easy decisions, and 31.3 on hard ones.

sections.title: 5.3 Why Nested Training Helps
sections.content: Shallow Exits Keep More of the Full Models Skill. Section 3.2 found that separately trained small models are degraded copies of the full model. Table 5 shows that nesting reduces this degradation rather than adding new skills. NESTONE is the k-layer exit. exit wins no more decisions of its own than M12 does (3.6% vs. 3.8%). Instead, it loses fewer of full32s correct decisions (23.4% vs. 26.5%), so its recall of full32s skill rises from 0.66 to 0.69. On decisions full32 is confident about, it is right 72.8% of the time, against 69.5% for M12. The 16layer exit shows the same pattern: recall rises from 0.79 to 0.81, and accuracy on confident decisions from 83.3% to 86.0%, with no more wins of its own (3.5% vs. 3.6%). This is the effect the selfdistillation term targets: the shallow exit imitates the full model and keeps more of what the full model knows. Deep Exits Stay Close to the Full Model. At 24 and 32 layers, the nested exits keep as much of full32s skill as M24 (recall 0.950.96 vs. 0.96), and their own wins (2.42.8%) are close to those of M24 (2.2%). Nesting neither adds nor removes skill at these depths. This matches Table 3, where the deep exits tie their separate counterparts. The benefit of nesting at depth is therefore cost, not accuracy: one checkpoint provides the 24-layer exit and the full model together, and the gate can choose between depths for each decision. Where Does NESTONE Write the Decision? Figure 4 shows that nested training shifts decision formation toward earlier layers, reversing the delay caused by plain fine-tuning. In the 32-layer exit, layers 016 account for half of the final margin (bootstrap range 1516), and layers 020 account for 80% (1920), compared with layers 20 and 23 in full32. The first 20 layers contribute 77% of the margin, versus 47% in full32, so the full model largely commits to its decision within the prefix shared by the 24-layer exit. Jointly ablating layers 2429 increases the margin by 4% and reduces accuracy by only 0.6 points. The 24-layer exit follows similar pattern: layers 1521 form its decision, with layer 20 alone contributing 48%. Thus, nested training concentrates decision formation in layers shared across deeper exits.

sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: We studied adaptive computation for System One decision-making in LLMs. Our analysis reveals that decisions primarily emerge in middle layers, with later layers contributing little additional information, and that smaller independently trained models largely replicate the full models decisions. Motivated by these findings, NESTONE jointly trains nested prefix sub-models via self-distillation and employs hidden-state gate for adaptive early exiting. Across three seeds, single checkpoint matches or outperforms independently trained models at all exit depths, improving 12-layer accuracy by 2.9 points and approaching the 32-layer model within 0.6 points at 24 layers. Adaptive exiting further reduces computation by 1627% on easy decisions without sacrificing accuracy, while retaining fixed-depth exits for harder cases. These results highlight the benefits of nested training for aligning shallow exits with full-model decisions. Future work will investigate end-to-end latency, gate calibration under real-world traffic, and scaling to larger models and finer-grained exits.
